A power saving below two-thirds for equal radicals of consecutive products

Ruiyi Zhang Independent Researcher, Columbia, Maryland, USA
Abstract.

Let F⁢(X)F(X) count positive integer pairs m<n≤Xm<n\leq X with rad⁡(m⁢(m+1))=rad⁡(n⁢(n+1))\operatorname{rad}(m(m+1))=\operatorname{rad}(n(n+1)). We prove F⁢(X)≪εX109/165+εF(X)\ll_{\varepsilon}X^{109/165+\varepsilon} for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, improving the earlier exponent 2/32/3. A four-corner parametrization divides these pairs into thirteen classes. Uniform estimates for those classes combine with a finite exponent calculation and one choice of error terms.

Key words and phrases:
radicals, consecutive integers, quadratic fibres, determinant method
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification:
Primary 11A25; Secondary 11D25, 11N37

1. Introduction

For a positive integer rr, let rad⁡(r)=∏p∣rp\operatorname{rad}(r)=\prod_{p\mid r}p. We count ordered pairs

F⁢(X)=#⁢{(m,n)∈ℤ>02:m<n≤X,rad⁡(m⁢(m+1))=rad⁡(n⁢(n+1))}.F(X)=\#\{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{2}:m<n\leq X,\ \operatorname{rad}(m(m+1))=% \operatorname{rad}(n(n+1))\}.
Theorem 1.1.

For every ε>0\varepsilon>0 and X≥2X\geq 2,

F⁢(X)≪εX109/165+ε.F(X)\ll_{\varepsilon}X^{109/165+\varepsilon}.

The exponent is 1/1651/165 below 2/32/3. Section 2 introduces the four-corner gcd coordinates. It also records the source-specific identities used here. The new part has three pieces: a first-match partition into thirteen disjoint populations, uniform estimates for its new rows, and a finite optimization of the long-shift remainder.

The minimum S0S_{0} below is the limiting minimum of the row savings. After the analytic loss β0\beta_{0} and a conservative long-row charge g0/4g_{0}/4, the proof retains the smaller saving displayed below.

The earlier result [1, Theorem 1] gives exponent 2/32/3 for this counting function. Its support-fibre lemma and low-radical estimate are used below; Appendix E states them and records the substitutions. The quotient-tail and Farey-spacing estimates in that paper are context only. They are not used. Two related papers by the author [2, 3] count primitive a⁢b⁢cabc triples, not the pairs counted here, and do not enter this proof.

At the chosen rational point, the minimum row saving is

S0=308695000000,g0=S0−1165=18677165000000.S_{0}=\frac{30869}{5000000},\qquad g_{0}=S_{0}-\frac{1}{165}=\frac{18677}{1650% 00000}.

The source-uniform estimates spend a total analytic loss β0=g0/16\beta_{0}=g_{0}/16. The long row has three finite corrections: geometric, interval, and high-degree. Beyond the common threshold each is at most g0/4g_{0}/4. We charge their maximum, not their sum. The remaining margin is

S0−β0−g04=1165+11⁢g016>1165.S_{0}-\beta_{0}-\frac{g_{0}}{4}=\frac{1}{165}+\frac{11g_{0}}{16}>\frac{1}{165}.

Sections 2–3 give the canonical source and the exact row partition. Sections 4–6 treat the outer, joint-corner, short-shift and intermediate rows. Section 7 handles the long row. Sections 8–10 allocate losses and sum the dyadic shells. The appendices contain the self-contained square-fibre proof, the application of the cited estimates, and the branch arithmetic. The use of AI tools is described after the appendices.

We use Heath–Brown’s published Lemma 2 under its stated bihomogeneous hypotheses. The fixed cubic branch uses the unnumbered theorem of Bombieri–Schmidt with its 1989 correction [6]. Appendix E states both inputs and records the applications. Reuss’s Theorem 1 [7] is the determinant-method input behind the low-radical estimate in [1]. That estimate is used here. Tao’s Lemma 2.10 gives a comparison with the square-fibre estimate of Appendix B. The proof uses that appendix theorem.

2. Canonical source and parameters

For an integer Y≥2Y\geq 2, let

ΩY={(m,n)∈ℤ>02:m<n≤Y,Y/2<n,rad⁡(m⁢(m+1))=rad⁡(n⁢(n+1))}.\Omega_{Y}=\{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{2}:m<n\leq Y,\ Y/2<n,\ \operatorname{rad% }(m(m+1))=\operatorname{rad}(n(n+1))\}.

An element of ΩY\Omega_{Y} is called a source pair. For each source pair define its four corner gcds by

A=gcd⁡(m,n),B=gcd⁡(m,n+1),C=gcd⁡(m+1,n),D=gcd⁡(m+1,n+1).A=\gcd(m,n),\quad B=\gcd(m,n+1),\quad C=\gcd(m+1,n),\quad D=\gcd(m+1,n+1).

These four integers are pairwise coprime. For example, a prime dividing AA and BB would divide both nn and n+1n+1. A prime dividing AA and CC would divide both mm and m+1m+1. The same two consecutive pairs settle the other four pairs. Each corner divides the two entries in its definition. Hence, by pairwise coprimality, A⁢B∣mAB\mid m, C⁢D∣m+1CD\mid m+1, A⁢C∣nAC\mid n, and B⁢D∣n+1BD\mid n+1. Define the positive integer residuals

a=mA⁢B,b=m+1C⁢D,c=nA⁢C,d=n+1B⁢D.a=\frac{m}{AB},\qquad b=\frac{m+1}{CD},\qquad c=\frac{n}{AC},\qquad d=\frac{n+% 1}{BD}.

The residuals are pairwise coprime. First, gcd⁡(a,b)=gcd⁡(c,d)=1\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(c,d)=1, since each pair divides consecutive integers. For the four cross pairs, divide the defining corner gcds. This gives

gcd⁡(B⁢a,C⁢c)=gcd⁡(A⁢a,D⁢d)=gcd⁡(D⁢b,A⁢c)=gcd⁡(C⁢b,B⁢d)=1,\gcd(Ba,Cc)=\gcd(Aa,Dd)=\gcd(Db,Ac)=\gcd(Cb,Bd)=1,

so gcd⁡(a,c)=gcd⁡(a,d)=gcd⁡(b,c)=gcd⁡(b,d)=1\gcd(a,c)=\gcd(a,d)=\gcd(b,c)=\gcd(b,d)=1 as well. The coordinates and mask are

(2.1) m=A⁢B⁢a,m+1=C⁢D⁢b,n=A⁢C⁢c,n+1=B⁢D⁢d,Z=A⁢B⁢C⁢D,R=rad⁡(Z),M=a⁢b⁢c⁢d,Kres=M/rad⁡(M),L=c⁢d−a⁢b,α=a⁢c,β=b⁢d,γ=a⁢d,δ=b⁢c,u=(m+n+1)/(B⁢C),t=(n−m)/(A⁢D),C⁢D⁢b−A⁢B⁢a=1,B⁢D⁢d−A⁢C⁢c=1.\begin{gathered}m=ABa,\quad m+1=CDb,\quad n=ACc,\quad n+1=BDd,\\ Z=ABCD,\quad R=\operatorname{rad}(Z),\quad M=abcd,\\ K_{\rm res}=M/\operatorname{rad}(M),\quad L=cd-ab,\\ \alpha=ac,\quad\beta=bd,\quad\gamma=ad,\quad\delta=bc,\\ u=(m+n+1)/(BC),\qquad t=(n-m)/(AD),\\ CDb-ABa=1,\qquad BDd-ACc=1.\end{gathered}

The four cross-gcd identities above will be used below. The radical condition is exactly rad⁡(M)∣Z\operatorname{rad}(M)\mid Z. If p∣ap\mid a, then p∣mp\mid m. Equality of the original radicals forces p∣np\mid n or p∣n+1p\mid n+1. Hence p∣Ap\mid A or p∣Bp\mid B. The other residuals give the corresponding corner. Conversely, every prime of ZZ divides both consecutive products. The mask ensures that no residual introduces a prime outside ZZ. Thus the common radical is

rad⁡(m⁢(m+1))=rad⁡(n⁢(n+1))=R.\operatorname{rad}(m(m+1))=\operatorname{rad}(n(n+1))=R.

gcd⁡(u,A⁢D)=gcd⁡(t,B⁢C)=1.\gcd(u,AD)=\gcd(t,BC)=1.

Theorem 3.1 (Exact partition).

The thirteen first-match sets in (3.1) are pairwise disjoint and have union ΩY\Omega_{Y}. On 5⁢W5W,

(3.2) s≥Yb0,Kres≤YΔexp,L≥Y1/3−l0,J,K≥Y1/3−j0.s\geq Y^{b_{0}},\qquad K_{\rm res}\leq Y^{\Delta_{\rm exp}},\qquad L\geq Y^{1/% 3-l_{0}},\qquad J,K\geq Y^{1/3-j_{0}}.
Proof.

The quantities in (3.1) are deterministic functions of the canonical source. Each of the first twelve rows is intersected with the complements of the preceding predicates. So these rows are disjoint. If s<Yb0s<Y^{b_{0}}, trichotomy gives exactly one of the 4⁢E,4⁢H,4⁢P4E,4H,4P predicates. Therefore their complement has s≥Yb0s\geq Y^{b_{0}}. ∎

4. Outer rows and inherited fibres

The small-radical input is Theorem 3 of [1]. Appendix E states it, and Appendix C records the shell substitution. With H=Y/2H=Y/2 and V=Y5/3−ϵ0V=Y^{5/3-\epsilon_{0}}, it gives

(4.1) #⁢{n:Y/2<n≤Y,rad⁡(n⁢(n+1))≤Y5/3−ϵ0}≪ηY2/3−S0+η.\#\{n:Y/2<n\leq Y,\ \operatorname{rad}(n(n+1))\leq Y^{5/3-\epsilon_{0}}\}\ll_{% \eta}Y^{2/3-S_{0}+\eta}.

The threshold in that application is large enough that Y≥4Y\geq 4 and Y1/3+ϵ0>4Y^{1/3+\epsilon_{0}}>4. These are exactly the required conditions H≥2H\geq 2 and V<H2V<H^{2}.

Let QsfQ_{\rm sf} be a positive squarefree integer. For a positive integer QQ, let ω⁢(Q)\omega(Q) denote the number of distinct prime divisors of QQ. Apply the support-fibre estimate [1, Lemma 2.1] with X=nX=n:

(4.2) #⁢{1≤m⁢<n:rad⁡(m⁢(m+1))∣⁢Qsf}≪ηY2⁢η⁢log⁡(2⁢Y).\#\{1\leq m<n:\operatorname{rad}(m(m+1))\mid Q_{\rm sf}\}\ll_{\eta}Y^{2\eta}% \log(2Y).

Here Qsf=rad⁡(n⁢(n+1))Q_{\rm sf}=\operatorname{rad}(n(n+1)) is squarefree and at most Y⁢(Y+1)Y(Y+1). The source equality of radicals gives the divisibility condition for every partner. The bound follows from 2ω⁢(Qsf)≪ηQsfη2^{\omega(Q_{\rm sf})}\ll_{\eta}Q_{\rm sf}^{\eta}. Choose the internal exponents smaller than the requested final ε\varepsilon. Absorbing the logarithm then proves the ORO_{R} row bound.

Proposition 4.1 (Five outer rows).

For every ε>0\varepsilon>0,

(4.3) #⁢OR,#⁢OM,#⁢Orad⁡M,#⁢Q⁢1\displaystyle\#O_{R},\ \#O_{M},\ \#O_{\operatorname{rad}M},\ \#Q1 ≪εY2/3−S0+ε,\displaystyle\ll_{\varepsilon}Y^{2/3-S_{0}+\varepsilon},

Proof.

The ORO_{R} estimate is (4.1) followed by the partner-fibre bound (4.2). We apply the latter with X=nX=n and with the squarefree common radical as QQ. The defining equality of radicals implies the required divisibility rad⁡(m⁢(m+1))∣Q\operatorname{rad}(m(m+1))\mid Q. Appendix B A uniform square-fibre bound

Tao’s Lemma 2.10 [8, Lemma 2.10] gives a related square-fibre bound. Appendix E states its hypotheses. The self-contained theorem below gives the fixed-ε\varepsilon, fixed-polynomial-height version used here. It assumes no uniform Pell-orbit or regulator bound.

Theorem B.1 (Uniform square fibres).

Fix A≥1A\geq 1. For every ε>0\varepsilon>0 there is a constant CA,εC_{A,\varepsilon} such that, for x≥2x\geq 2, positive integers a,b≤xAa,b\leq x^{A}, and a nonzero integer hh with |h|≤xA|h|\leq x^{A},

(B.1) #⁢{(n,m)∈ℤ>02:a⁢n2+h=b⁢m2,n≤x}≤CA,ε⁢xε.\#\{(n,m)\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{2}:an^{2}+h=bm^{2},\ n\leq x\}\leq C_{A,% \varepsilon}x^{\varepsilon}.

The constant is independent of a,b,ha,b,h. The exponent AA is fixed.

Lemma B.2 (Divisor bound).

For every δ>0\delta>0, τdiv⁢(N)≪δNδ\tau_{\mathrm{div}}(N)\ll_{\delta}N^{\delta} for N≥1N\geq 1.

Proof.

For primes p≥21/δp\geq 2^{1/\delta}, j+1≤2j≤pδ⁢jj+1\leq 2^{j}\leq p^{\delta j}. There are finitely many smaller primes. For each of them supj≥0(j+1)⁢p−δ⁢j<∞\sup_{j\geq 0}(j+1)p^{-\delta j}<\infty. Multiply over the prime factorization. ∎

Lemma B.3 (Roots of a quadratic congruence).

If D≥2D\geq 2 is squarefree and M≥1M\geq 1, then

(B.2) #⁢{rmodM:r2≡D(modM)}≤4⋅2ω⁢(M).\#\{r\bmod M:r^{2}\equiv D\pmod{M}\}\leq 4\cdot 2^{\omega(M)}.

For M=1M=1 there is one residue class.

Proof.

It suffices to count roots modulo prime powers. For an odd prime p∣Dp\mid D, there is one root modulo pp and none modulo pep^{e}, e≥2e\geq 2. Here a root would have valuation at least one. Its square would then have valuation at least two. If p∤Dp\nmid D, a root r0r_{0} is a unit. For any other root rr, pe∣(r−r0)⁢(r+r0)p^{e}\mid(r-r_{0})(r+r_{0}). The two factors are not both divisible by pp. So r≡r0r\equiv r_{0} or −r0(modpe)-r_{0}\pmod{p^{e}}. There are at most two roots.

Let p=2p=2. If DD is even, squarefreeness gives D≡2(mod4)D\equiv 2\pmod{4}. Then there are no roots modulo 2e2^{e} for e≥2e\geq 2, and at most one modulo 2. Let DD be odd and let r0r_{0} be one root. Multiplication by r0−1r_{0}^{-1} injects the roots into solutions of z2≡1(mod2e)z^{2}\equiv 1\pmod{2^{e}}. For e=1,2e=1,2 there are at most two. Let e≥3e\geq 3. Then zz is odd, and exactly one of z−1,z+1z-1,z+1 is divisible by 22 but not 44. Their product is divisible by 2e2^{e}. So the other is divisible by 2e−12^{e-1}. Hence z≡1z\equiv 1 or −1(mod2e−1)-1\pmod{2^{e-1}}. This gives at most four classes modulo 2e2^{e}. The Chinese remainder theorem multiplies these local bounds, and (B.2) follows. ∎

Lemma B.4 (Spacing in one norm class).

Let D≥2D\geq 2 be squarefree, N∈ℤ∖{0}N\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}, and H≥1H\geq 1. The number of positive integral solutions of

X2−D⁢Y2=N,X+Y⁢D≤HX^{2}-DY^{2}=N,\qquad X+Y\sqrt{D}\leq H

is at most

(B.3) 4⁢τdiv⁢(|N|)2⁢(1+log⁡Hlog⁡(2+3)).4\tau_{\mathrm{div}}(|N|)^{2}\left(1+\frac{\log H}{\log(2+\sqrt{3})}\right).
Proof.

Put g=gcd⁡(X,Y)g=\gcd(X,Y). Then g2∣Ng^{2}\mid N. For each of at most τdiv⁢(|N|)\tau_{\mathrm{div}}(|N|) choices of gg, set U=X/gU=X/g, V=Y/gV=Y/g, and N0=N/g2N_{0}=N/g^{2}. The pair (U,V)(U,V) is primitive. Also gcd⁡(V,|N0|)=1\gcd(V,|N_{0}|)=1. Otherwise, by the norm equation, a common prime would divide U2U^{2}, hence UU. This contradicts primitivity. Thus r=U⁢V−1(mod|N0|)r=UV^{-1}\pmod{|N_{0}|} is defined and satisfies r2≡Dr^{2}\equiv D. For modulus one use its unique class. By (B.2), there are at most 4⁢τdiv⁢(|N|)4\tau_{\mathrm{div}}(|N|) such classes.

Take two solutions in one class. Write αi=Ui+Vi⁢D>1\alpha_{i}=U_{i}+V_{i}\sqrt{D}>1. Direct multiplication gives

(B.4) α1α2=s+t⁢D,s=U1⁢U2−D⁢V1⁢V2N0,t=V1⁢U2−U1⁢V2N0.\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\alpha_{2}}=s+t\sqrt{D},\quad s=\frac{U_{1}U_{2}-DV_{1}V_{2}% }{N_{0}},\quad t=\frac{V_{1}U_{2}-U_{1}V_{2}}{N_{0}}.

Here s,ts,t are the integer coefficients of this norm-one quotient. This local tt is unrelated to either source shift. Both numerators are divisible by N0N_{0}. To see this, work modulo |N0||N_{0}| and use Ui≡r⁢ViU_{i}\equiv rV_{i} and r2≡Dr^{2}\equiv D. Hence s,ts,t are integers even when N0<0N_{0}<0. The quotient has norm one. Let α1/α2>1\alpha_{1}/\alpha_{2}>1. Its conjugate is the positive reciprocal. Thus s=(α1/α2+α2/α1)/2>1s=(\alpha_{1}/\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{2}/\alpha_{1})/2>1. Since ss is an integer, s≥2s\geq 2, and

α1α2=s+s2−1≥2+3.\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\alpha_{2}}=s+\sqrt{s^{2}-1}\geq 2+\sqrt{3}.

Remark B.5.

Every use has positive coefficients and a nonzero shift. The coefficients and the shift have fixed polynomial height. One variable is bounded, and the equation then bounds the other. No discriminant-dependent constant or fundamental-unit estimate occurs.

The unnumbered theorem of Bombieri–Schmidt [5, pp. 69–70] reads as follows. Let F∈ℤ⁢[x,y]F\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y] be an irreducible binary form of degree r≥3r\geq 3 and let h≥1h\geq 1. Then the number of primitive integer solutions of |F⁢(x,y)|=h|F(x,y)|=h is at most CBS⁢r1+ω⁢(h)C_{\rm BS}r^{1+\omega(h)}, with absolute CBSC_{\rm BS}. The 1989 correction to their proof of Lemma 7 [6] changes no hypothesis of this theorem. In Section 6 the form is the irreducible binary cubic c1⁢x3−c2⁢z3c_{1}x^{3}-c_{2}z^{3}. Its content and the common divisor of x,zx,z are removed first. The right side is nonzero. The theorem gives O⁢(31+ω⁢(|h|))O(3^{1+\omega(|h|)}) primitive solutions. The reducible case occurs when both coprime coefficients are cubes. Section 6 counts it separately by factoring the difference of cubes.
